candidates.description: Replace the per‑row `invoiceRepo.countByCustomerId` calls with a single batched query that returns counts for all customer IDs in the result set. The service collects the customer IDs from the recent‑payment rows, runs a single `SELECT i.customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM invoice i WHERE i.customer_id IN (:ids) GROUP BY i.customer_id` query, builds a map, and populates `RecentPaymentSummaryDto` using that map instead of invoking the count method in the loop.
candidates.predicted_effect: rows examined drop from ~726 630 200 (total across N+1 counts) to ~32 931 (single grouped count scan) per request
candidates.sql_after: SELECT cp.id, cp.customer_id, c.name, cp.paid_on, cp.amount, cp.method, ic.cnt FROM customer_payment cp JOIN customer c ON cp.customer_id = c.id LEFT JOIN (SELECT i.customer_id, COUNT(*) cnt FROM invoice i GROUP BY i.customer_id) ic ON cp.customer_id = ic.customer_id WHERE cp.method = ? ORDER BY cp.paid_on DESC, cp.id DESC LIMIT ? OFFSET ?
what_could_break: If the IN‑list of customer IDs is larger than MySQL's limit for a single query, the batched count could fail.
Changes to the ordering or pagination logic must stay identical; any mismatch could alter the contract.
If a customer has no invoices, the left join must produce a null count; the code must treat null as zero.
